sections.figure_idea: A simple diagram with Chapters 1-7 in one box and Chapter 8 in its own box, with a few labelled arrows showing where Chapter 8 reaches back, for example to 250.94 for the intersystem bonding termination.
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 90 explains how the Code is organized, and 90.3 draws a line around Chapter 8. In plain terms, the general rules in Chapters 1 through 7 do not automatically apply to a communications installation. They apply only where Chapter 8 itself points back to them, or where a specific article in this chapter says so. That is why a rule you know well from power wiring cannot simply be carried over to a phone, data, or coax job. The reach-backs Chapter 8 actually makes include:
• 250.94 — the intersystem bonding termination that communications grounding lands on
• 300.4(D) and 300.11 — pulled in by 800.24 for protecting and supporting cable
• 300.22 — the air-handling space rules the chapter's cable rules reference
sections.why_it_exists: Crews carry habits from one system to another, and the wrong habit cuts both ways: it over-builds a comm job with power rules nobody asked for, or it skips a protection that Chapter 8 does require because the power article was never opened. The 90.3 line keeps every system judged by its own rules, and it tells you exactly where to look when the two worlds touch.
sections.on_the_job: When a power-wiring rule and a Chapter 8 job seem to collide, do not assume the power rule wins. Open the communications article first and look for a reference back to Chapters 1 through 7. On a Marion Oaks rough-in the crew argued over whether the 1¼ in stud-boring rule reaches a coax run. It does — not because Chapter 3 reaches across, but because 800.24 points to 300.4(D). If Chapter 8 is silent, ask the lead or the AHJ instead of inventing a bridge.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: all of Chapter 3 applies to communications work because the cables run through the same studs. Wrong. Under 90.3, Chapters 1 through 7 apply to a Chapter 8 installation only where Chapter 8 specifically references them — the reference is the bridge, not the shared wall cavity.

sections.title: Article 800 — General requirements for communications systems
sections.plain_explanation: Article 800 is the general article that was new in the 2020 edition. It gathers the rules that used to be repeated in almost every communications article — things like workmanship, abandoned cable, fire spread, cables entering a building, bonding and grounding, separation from power, and cable listing — and states them once. Those general rules then apply to the specific systems in Articles 805, 820, 830, and 840, unless one of those articles changes them. Article 810, antennas, is the exception: it stands apart from Article 800 and carries its own rules.
sections.on_the_job: Read Article 800 first on any communications job, then read the specific article for the system you are installing. Most inspection failures Sharma would hit in this chapter — no bond at the entrance, cable mixed with power, dead cable left in a ceiling — are Article 800 failures, not failures of the specific system article.

sections.title: Scope of the general article
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 800 is the general article for Chapter 8. It states the requirements every communications system in the chapter shares, and it works together with the specific articles, so a telephone circuit, a CATV coax run, and a broadband entrance all start here for their shared rules.
• 800 — the general rules themselves
• 805 — communications circuits
• 810 — radio and television equipment
• 820 — community antenna television (CATV) coaxial systems
• 830 — network-powered broadband systems
• 840 — premises-powered broadband systems
Article 800 does not cover the utility's own plant under the utility's exclusive control, which Article 90 leaves outside the Code. The customer's side of the demarcation point is where this book's work lives.
sections.why_it_exists: Most Chapter 8 arguments on a job are really scope arguments: whose cable is it, and whose rules judge it? If the line between the provider's plant and the customer's wiring is fuzzy, the protector, the bonding and the separation work can fall between two crews, with each side sure the other one owns it. 800.1 draws the line so the entrance gets built once, by the crew the Code actually covers.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call at a Winter Park home, find the demarcation point first — the provider's box on the side of the house. Everything on the customer side is fair game for Chapter 8 rules; the provider's network on the other side is theirs. When the provider's installer and Sharma's crew disagree about a bond or a cable, this scope line usually settles whose rules apply: Sharma bonds the protector and runs the inside Cat 6 and coax, and the buried drop on the street side of the demarc stays the provider's problem.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that Article 800 covers telephone circuits only. It is the general article for the whole chapter — its rules ride on top of CATV, broadband and radio/TV work too. The reverse trap also shows up: applying Article 800 to the utility's own plant under its exclusive control, which the Code does not cover at all.

sections.title: Definitions that belong to this chapter
sections.plain_explanation: Some words in this chapter carry Code definitions, and this section holds the ones communications work turns on. Two do daily duty. The point of entrance is the point where a communications wire or cable comes into the building from outside — through a wall, a floor, or a grounded metal raceway that extends it — and almost every entrance rule in the chapter is measured from it. Abandoned communications cable, defined here, is cable that is not terminated at equipment and not identified for future use with a tag, which is the test 800.25 then applies.
sections.on_the_job: Before arguing about where a protector, bond, or 50 ft limit lands, settle where the point of entrance is — the wall penetration, or the end of the grounded entrance conduit if one extends it. And when a dead cable is disputed, run the definition: terminated, or tagged for future use? If neither, it is abandoned.

sections.title: How Article 800 works with the other articles
sections.plain_explanation: Article 800 is a layer, not a replacement. Its general rules apply across the communications articles unless a specific article modifies them, and other NEC articles apply to a communications job only where Chapter 8 references them. One practical example: reconditioned communications equipment is pulled back to the general marking rules of Chapter 1 through this section. Another is grounding: Chapter 8 repeatedly sends you to the intersystem bonding termination described in 250.94, instead of restating it. So the order of work is always the same: general rule first, specific article second, referenced article only where the chapter points.
sections.on_the_job: A Kissimmee office rough-in mixes three Chapter 8 systems in one ceiling: 805 circuits for the phone system, 820 coax for the TV drops, and 830 broadband at the demarc. Work the layers in order on each one: 800 for the general rule, the specific article (805, 820, 830, or 840) for anything that changes it, then any article Chapter 8 points you to. Do not skip straight to a Chapter 3 wiring method and assume it governs a communications cable.

sections.why_it_exists: Chapter 8 systems carry signals, not building power, and their hazards are different — surge energy at entrances, fire spread along cable jackets, abandoned cable adding fuel. If every power-wiring rule in the earlier chapters applied by default, the communications articles would drown in exceptions. The layer design keeps one general rulebook for all communications work, lets each system article adjust it, and borrows an outside rule only by name.

sections.title: Keep the ceiling panels removable — cable cannot block access
sections.plain_explanation: Access to electrical equipment must not be denied by an accumulation of communications wires and cables that prevents removal of panels, including suspended-ceiling panels. In plain terms, the tiles of a suspended ceiling are an access door to the junction boxes, disconnects, and other electrical equipment above them. A bundle of data cable draped across the grid so that a panel cannot be lifted out fails this section, even if every cable in the bundle is the right type, properly supported, and properly bonded. The rule is not about the cable — it is about keeping the access the ceiling was designed to give.
sections.on_the_job: Route and support the runs so any ceiling panel can still be lifted and slid aside: bundles on their own hangers or J-hooks above the grid, never resting on the tiles, never piled across the panel below a box or disconnect someone will need to reach. If you cannot lift the tile, neither can the next electrician — and the inspector will try the tile nearest the equipment.

sections.title: Doing the work neatly and protecting the cable
sections.figure_idea: A photo-style drawing of a stud bay with a centered bored hole, a supported Cat 6 and coax run, and a red X over a cable zip-tied to an EMT run.
sections.plain_explanation:
This section requires communications work to be done in a neat, workmanlike way, and it ties cable installation to basic protection against physical damage.
• Circuits and equipment are installed in a neat and workmanlike manner — sloppy low-voltage work is still a code violation even though the voltage is low.
• Cables installed exposed on ceilings and sidewalls are supported by the building structure so normal building use cannot damage them, secured with straps, staples, cable ties, hangers or similar fittings that do not damage the cable.
• The installation also conforms to 300.4(D) — cable run through or parallel to framing keeps 1¼ in from the edge of the wood member, or gets a steel plate — and to 300.11 on securing and supporting.
• Nonmetallic cable ties and accessories used in plenum spaces must be listed as having low smoke and heat release properties.
Cables must never hang off other systems: not a power raceway, not a sprinkler pipe, not a ceiling grid wire that is not part of the support system.
sections.why_it_exists: Low voltage fools people into thinking the work cannot hurt anyone, so it gets draped, pinched and abandoned in ceilings. Then a drywall screw nicks the jacket, a ceiling tile change saws through an unsupported run, and the phone, data or alarm path the building counts on is dead — sometimes silently, until the day it is needed. Neat, supported, protected cable is what survives the other trades.
sections.on_the_job: Roughing in a three-bedroom home in Marion Oaks: dress the runs, support them on their own supports, and keep holes centered in studs the way you would for power cable — 1¼ in or more from the stud edge on 14 Cat 6 and coax home runs. Never hang a communications cable from a power raceway, a sprinkler pipe, or a ceiling grid wire that is not part of the support system. The one run a helper zip-tied to a sprinkler line on this job got cut and re-pulled before insulation. A neat rough-in is also the fastest one to inspect.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that a communications cable may rest on the ceiling grid and tie to the grid wires, because it is 'only low voltage.' Wrong twice: 800.24 sends support to 300.11, and the grid is not a cable support unless it is part of an identified support system. The voltage on the cable does not soften the mechanical rules.

sections.title: Abandoned cable has to come out
sections.plain_explanation: A communications cable that is no longer terminated at equipment, and is not tagged for future use, counts as abandoned. The accessible part of abandoned cable must be removed, because dead cable is fuel in a ceiling or shaft and it confuses every crew that comes later. A cable you honestly plan to reuse can stay, but only if it carries a durable tag saying so, suited to the environment it sits in. Cable hidden inside a concealed raceway is not treated as accessible, so the removal duty is aimed at what a crew can actually reach.
sections.on_the_job: On a remodel or a tenant finish-out, walk the ceiling before you add anything. Pull out dead coax and old phone cable you can reach, and tag any spare you are keeping with what it is and where it goes. 'We might use it someday' with no tag does not count.

sections.title: Slowing the spread of fire and smoke
sections.plain_explanation:
Communications cables, raceways, and cable routing assemblies must be installed so they do not noticeably increase how fire or the products of combustion can spread through hollow spaces, shafts, and air-handling paths.
• Where a cable or raceway passes through a fire-resistance-rated wall, floor, partition, or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved method that restores the rating.
• The firestop has to match the assembly and the cable type — a listed system, putty, or collars made for that penetration.
This mirrors the general firestopping rule in Chapter 3 (300.21), restated here because Chapter 8 stands on its own.
sections.on_the_job: Every poke through a rated assembly gets firestopped — putty, collars, or a listed system matched to the cable type and the assembly. On a Florida retail buildout, a bundle of two dozen Cat 6 and four coax through a 1-hour corridor wall gets a listed firestop system sized for that bundle, not a smear of caulk. Do not leave an oversized hole stuffed with scrap insulation and call it done. In Florida commercial work this is one of the most common communications corrections on a final inspection.

sections.title: Never run a cable hotter than its rating
sections.plain_explanation: No wire or cable may be used in such a manner that its operating temperature exceeds the temperature rating of the wire or cable. It is a one-sentence general rule — the Chapter 8 counterpart of the temperature limitation the rest of the Code puts on conductors — and the heat it guards against can come from anywhere: a hot attic or boiler room, a sun-baked exterior run, or the cable's own load, since communications cables that deliver power to devices warm up from the inside, and the middle of a fat bundle warms up most. The cable types in 800.179 are built around temperature — suitable for at least 60°C, with any higher rating marked — and this section is the installation rule that says the rating has to be respected in the field, not just on the reel.
sections.on_the_job: Think about heat before you bundle. A thick bundle of powered Ethernet cable in a Florida attic is the classic trap: the room is already hot and the center of the bundle runs far hotter than the air around it. Split oversized powered bundles, keep runs out of the hottest part of the attic where the layout allows, and never bury communications cable in insulation or strap it against a heat source and assume the jacket rating will save it.

sections.title: Overhead wires and cables coming into a building
sections.plain_explanation: Overhead communications wires and cables that enter a building have clearance and separation rules where they cross roofs and where they run near the power service. Communications drops must keep a vertical clearance of at least 8 ft above roofs they pass over, with limited exceptions. Where a power service drop of 750 volts or less runs above and parallel to a communications or coax drop, the two need at least 12 in of separation through the span and at the building attachment, provided the power conductors are insulated and at least 40 in of clearance is kept between the two services at the pole.
sections.on_the_job: Before you set a ladder, look up: check the comm drop's height over the roof and its distance from the power drop at the wall and back at the pole. Never use the power service mast to support a communications drop. If the existing drop sags into the power drop, that is a provider call, not something to fix by pulling it tighter yourself.

sections.title: Underground cables where power is also present
sections.plain_explanation: Underground communications wires and cables that share a manhole, handhole, or similar enclosure with electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors must be kept apart from those conductors by a suitable barrier. The point is simple: a space where a worker may reach in and grab a cable cannot mix exposed power conductors with communications cable as if they were the same system. The barrier has to be permanent and suitable, not a scrap of cardboard or a cable draped to the far side.
sections.why_it_exists: A handhole is dark, wet and crowded, and a worker reaching in cannot tell a communications cable from a power conductor by feel. If a jacket is nicked or a power conductor faults, the 'harmless' cable in the same space can carry line voltage to the next person who grabs it — possibly a telephone tech who never expected voltage at all. The barrier keeps two systems that share a hole from ever sharing a touch.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma rarely opens manholes, but the same thinking applies at underground entrances and pull points on light-commercial work. On a Clermont strip plaza, the crew opened a handhole to pull a camera feed and found the existing comm cable lying across the lot-lighting conductors with no barrier at all. Do not just close the lid — report it and get the separation corrected before the new cable goes in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that draping the communications cable to the far side of the manhole is separation. Wrong. 800.47 wants a suitable barrier — a permanent, physical separation built into the enclosure — not distance by habit that disappears the first time someone re-dresses the cables.

sections.title: Grounding a metal conduit that carries the entrance cable
sections.plain_explanation: When the communications entrance wire or cable arrives inside a metal conduit, the conduit stops being just a sleeve. Section 800.49 requires that metal conduit to be connected, by a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor, to a grounding electrode — or to the building grounding electrode system where one exists — using the connection points given in 800.100(B). First choice on that list is the intersystem bonding termination; after that come the building's grounding electrode system and the other accessible points the section names, and in a building with no grounding means at all, an electrode installed for the purpose. A floating metal entrance conduit can sit at a very different potential from the building during a surge, which is exactly what the bond prevents.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Garden house, the provider's entrance cable comes down the wall in a 3/4 in EMT sleeve to the demarc box. Before the provider's appointment, we set a bonding clamp on the EMT and ran the bond about 8 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main — a listed 800.100(B) point, not the water pipe that happened to be closer. Plastic conduit would not need the bond, but it also would not extend the point of entrance the way a grounded metal raceway can, so the metal sleeve plus its bond is the better entrance.
sections.why_it_exists: The entrance conduit is a long piece of metal that starts outside the building, where lightning and utility surges arrive, and ends inside next to grounded equipment. Left floating, it can charge to a different voltage than everything around it and flash across to the nearest grounded metal — or to a person touching it. Bonding ties it to the same earth reference, so the whole entrance rises and falls together.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is landing the conduit bond on the nearest water pipe because metal is metal. Section 800.49 sends you to the connection points in 800.100(B) — the intersystem bonding termination first, then the building grounding system points the section lists. A random pipe may not be bonded to anything. Second trap: skipping the bond because the cable inside is fiber. The rule is about the metal conduit, not the signal inside it.
inspection_fails: Metal entrance conduit left floating — no bonding conductor or clamp installed (800.49).
Conduit bond landed on a nearby water pipe or a receptacle ground instead of an 800.100(B) connection point.
Bonding conductor smaller than 14 AWG, or run long and looping — 800.100(A) sets the floor and wants the run short; at a dwelling it may not exceed 20 ft.
Building with no grounding system bonded to a short scrap rod — 800.100(B) describes the purpose electrode as at least 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter.

sections.title: Keeping communications cable away from lightning protection
sections.plain_explanation: Where it is practicable, communications wires and cables on a building, including coax, are to be kept at least 6 ft away from lightning protection system conductors. A lightning down conductor carries an enormous surge for a few microseconds, and a communications cable run alongside it can pick up enough of that energy by induction to destroy equipment or start a fire inside. Where 6 ft genuinely cannot be had, the Code points to the sideflash calculation approach in the lightning protection standard rather than a guess.
sections.on_the_job: Florida is lightning country, so this one is not theoretical here. On any building with air terminals and down leads — churches, schools, larger custom homes — route the data and coax entrances to a different wall or corner whenever you can. If the only entrance is beside a down lead, raise it with the lead before the rough-in, not at final.
sections.figure_idea: A building corner sketch with a lightning down lead on one face, the communications entrance moved to the adjacent face, and a 6 ft dimension between the two paths.
sections.florida_note: Florida has more lightning than any other state; AHJs and insurers here take separation from lightning protection conductors seriously. Confirm the local position where a building has an existing lightning protection system.

sections.title: Bonding and grounding at the entrance — the heart of Chapter 8
sections.plain_explanation: This is the section the whole chapter hangs on. It covers how communications cables and primary protectors get bonded and grounded: the metallic parts that arrive from outside — cable sheaths, protector grounds, coax shields handled under their own articles — must be tied to the building's grounding system at the entrance. The bonding or grounding conductor has its own rules for material, size, and length, and for where it is allowed to land, which the next three pages break out. Done right, a surge arriving on a phone line or coax shield is carried to the same earth reference as the power service, so the two systems rise and fall together instead of sparking across to each other.
sections.on_the_job: Pick the protector and grounding-block location to keep this conductor as short and straight as you can. Land it at the intersystem bonding termination when one is there — that device exists precisely for this job (see 250.94, item L-060). Photograph the finished bond; it is the first thing a communications inspector looks for.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 puts the meter outside with the panel directly behind it inside, where the house allows. That same service spot is where the intersystem bonding termination belongs, so plan the communications bond to land at the service, not at a random rod driven by the cable installer.
sections.figure_idea: A house service wall in elevation: meter and panel back to back, an intersystem bonding termination beside the meter, and short bonding conductors arriving from the phone protector and the coax grounding block.

sections.title: The bonding conductor itself — material, size, and length
sections.plain_explanation: The conductor that bonds the protector or cable sheath has to be copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, solid or stranded, and listed for the purpose, with the insulation choices the section allows. It cannot be smaller than 14 AWG, and its current-carrying capacity has to be at least that of the metallic sheath or protected conductor it serves — but it never has to be larger than 6 AWG. It must be run as short as practicable, and in a one- or two-family dwelling it cannot exceed 20 ft. Where it runs in a metal raceway, that raceway has to be bonded at both ends, and the conductor should run in as straight a line as practicable and be protected from physical damage.
sections.on_the_job: Measure before you mount the protector: if the run to a legal landing point is over 20 ft at a house, move the protector or use the separate-electrode option on the next pages instead of stretching the conductor. Keep bends gentle and few — a surge does not like corners any more than the inspector does. Fourteen AWG is the floor, not a target; when in doubt, the sheath size governs.

sections.title: Where the bonding conductor is allowed to land
sections.plain_explanation: This part lists, in order, the places the entrance bonding or grounding conductor may terminate. First choice is the intersystem bonding termination, if the building has one. Without one, it lands on the building's grounding electrode system or one of the accessible grounding points the section names, such as the grounding electrode conductor or the service equipment enclosure, following the exact list in the printed section. In a building with no grounding means at all, it lands on an electrode installed for the purpose — a rod at least 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter is the minimum the section describes for that case.
sections.on_the_job: Use the first landing point on the list that the building actually has, and use the nearest accessible one. Do not land the bond on a random receptacle ground, a plumbing vent, or a rod you cannot prove is bonded to the power system. Item L-060 (250.94) explains the termination device itself.
sections.figure_idea: A decision ladder graphic: intersystem bonding termination at the top, then the building grounding electrode system points, then a new electrode at the bottom for buildings with no grounding means.

sections.title: Bonding a separate communications electrode back to the power system
sections.plain_explanation: Sometimes the bonding conductor cannot stay inside its length limit — the classic house case is the exception that lets a separate ground rod be driven for the communications system when the run would pass 20 ft. That separate electrode is never allowed to stand alone. It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system with a conductor no smaller than 6 AWG. Two unbonded earth connections at one house are worse than one, because a surge can put thousands of volts between them, right across the equipment inside.
sections.on_the_job: If you drive a rod for the phone or coax entrance, the job is not finished until the 6 AWG bond back to the power grounding system is in. The same 6 AWG bonding rule shows up again for antennas in 810.21(J) and for CATV in 820.100(D) — learn it once, use it three times.

sections.title: Grounding the primary protector at a mobile home
sections.plain_explanation: A mobile home gets its own version of the 800.100 grounding recipe, because the power service usually is not on the home itself — under 550.32(A) the service equipment or disconnecting means sits nearby, in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall. Where that equipment is in place, the primary protector is grounded and bonded into that grounding arrangement as 800.100 describes. Where there is no mobile home service equipment or grounded disconnect in sight and within 30 ft, 800.106(A) sends the grounding to the electrode options in 800.100(B)(3) — the same list used at a building that has no intersystem bonding termination and no grounding means. Either way, 800.106(B) adds a step an ordinary house does not need: the protector's grounding terminal must be bonded to the mobile home's metal frame, or to the grounding terminal the home provides, with copper not smaller than 12 AWG, so the telephone ground and the frame the occupants touch can never sit at different voltages in a surge. This section is also the reason the 6 AWG bond-back rule in 800.100(D) carries an exception for mobile homes — at a mobile home, 800.106 replaces it.
sections.on_the_job: On a manufactured-home call, find the pedestal or disconnect first. If it is in sight and within 30 ft, ground the protector into that system — and still add the 12 AWG copper bond to the home's frame or grounding terminal. If the disconnect is farther away, or there is no grounded disconnect to work from, you are on the 800.100(B)(3) electrode list, and the frame bond is still required. Do not skip the frame bond because the protector 'has its own ground rod': a rod alone does not tie the phone ground to the frame.
sections.figure_idea: A mobile home with its power pedestal nearby: the protector at the entrance grounded into the pedestal system, with the 12 AWG bond drawn from the protector to the home's frame; beside it, the same home with the pedestal far away and a local electrode driven at the home.

sections.title: Raceways and cable routing assemblies for communications
sections.plain_explanation: Communications wires and cables may be run in communications raceways and cable routing assemblies, as long as both are listed and chosen for the space they serve — plenum, riser, or general-purpose — under the application tables in 800.154. The raceway levels track the cable levels in 800.179 and the listing rules in 800.182, and a point from 800.182 is worth memorizing here: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it, so a plenum raceway in an air-handling space still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable. Chapter 9 conduit-fill rules do not govern ordinary communications cables in these raceways. The section keeps one exception: medium-power network-powered broadband cables. In other words, a listed low-voltage raceway is its own wiring method here; do not borrow a Chapter 3 conduit rule and assume it decides the question.
sections.on_the_job: On a light-commercial job in Kissimmee — a small medical office — the data runs cross an air-handling ceiling, so the spec is plenum-level raceway with CMP cable inside; the run down the shaft to the first floor is riser level with CMR. We kept the manufacturer's fill guidance for the cable routing assembly even though Chapter 9 fill percentages are not the governing rule — the listing still expects the cable supported and not crushed. And one boundary to respect: if the job is really Class 2 or Class 3 control wiring, you are in Article 725 (Chapter 7), not here.
sections.why_it_exists: The raceway levels exist because of fire and smoke, not electricity. A pathway that runs through an air-handling ceiling or a vertical shaft is a ready-made route for smoke to travel between spaces, so the pathway and the cable in it are both rated for the space. The fill exception exists for the opposite reason: a medium-power broadband cable carries real power alongside the signal, so it is treated more like a power cable than a whisper of data.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps meet on this page. First: the raceway is plenum-rated, so the CM cable inside it is fine in the plenum. No — 800.182 is explicit that the raceway does not upgrade the cable; each is matched to the space on its own. Second: applying Chapter 9 conduit-fill percentages to a listed communications raceway. Chapter 9 fill does not govern ordinary communications cables here — the only exception the section keeps is medium-power network-powered broadband cable.

sections.title: Installing cables inside the building — ducts, plenums, and risers
sections.plain_explanation: This long section is the inside-the-building installation rulebook for communications cable. Cables in ducts made for environmental air follow the duct rules it references, and cables in other air-handling spaces (plenums) must be the plenum types allowed there. Vertical runs that pass through one or more floors — risers — need riser-rated cable, or one of the protected alternatives the section lists, such as cable in a metal raceway or a fireproof shaft with firestops at each floor. One- and two-family dwellings get their own, more relaxed list, which is why house work and commercial work part company here. The section also carries a quiet but important marking rule: cables installed inside must be listed, and a voltage rating is not to be marked on a communications cable, because that marking invites someone to treat it as power wire.
sections.on_the_job: Before rough-in, ask one question per run: is this space moving air, or does this run pass a floor? A yes to the first means CMP; a yes to the second means CMR or a listed protected path. At a house, CM or CMX from the dwelling list is normally the right shelf to shop from.
sections.figure_idea: A three-panel figure: a plenum ceiling space labelled CMP, a vertical shaft between floors labelled CMR, and a same-floor office run labelled CM/CMG.

sections.title: Separation from power — the section in one view
sections.plain_explanation: This is the separation rule the inspection-prep notes pointed at, re-checked for this book: communications cables must be kept apart from electric light, power, Class 1, and non-power-limited fire alarm conductors. The rule has two halves. The first half governs sharing a raceway, box, or enclosure; the second half governs running alongside power wiring in open space, where the headline number is 2 in. A third part forbids using the outside of a raceway as a support for communications cable. The next two pages take the halves one at a time, because this is the single most-cited communications rule on Sharma's kind of work.
sections.on_the_job: Keep low-voltage cable out of power boxes and power raceways unless a listed barrier setup on the next page genuinely applies. Do not strap, tape, or tie a data or coax run to the outside of a conduit for support. When an inspector says 'separation,' this section is what they mean — and yes, the distance is 2 in, confirmed against the 2020 text and commentary, not the larger figures in some exam-prep sheets.
sections.figure_idea: An overview strip showing three scenes: same box (barrier needed), open parallel run (2 in gap), and a cable tied to a conduit (marked not permitted).

sections.title: Sharing a raceway, box, or enclosure with power
sections.plain_explanation: Communications conductors are not permitted in the same raceway, box, or enclosure as electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors as a general rule. The exceptions are narrow. Sharing is allowed where the two systems are separated by a permanent barrier or a listed divider, and power conductors may be brought into a communications enclosure only to feed the communications equipment itself, routed inside the enclosure to keep at least 1/4 in (6 mm) of separation from the communications wiring (800.133(A)(1), Exception No. 2). A shared box with a listed divider is a designed product, not two cables stuffed into one handy box.
sections.on_the_job: Default answer on site: separate boxes, separate raceways. If a plan shows a divided box, verify the divider is the listed one made for that box before rough-in, not after the drywall is up. The 1/4 in (6 mm) figure inside an equipment enclosure is not permission to mix systems in a junction box.

sections.title: The 2-inch separation in open runs
sections.plain_explanation: Where communications conductors run near power or Class 1 conductors outside a shared enclosure, they must be separated by at least 2 in. That 2 in can be provided by space alone, or by one of the constructions the section recognizes — for example, where the power conductors are inside a raceway or a metal-sheathed, armored, nonmetallic-sheathed, or UF cable assembly, or where the communications cable is in its own raceway, the bare 2 in spacing is not demanded because the sheath or raceway already provides the separation. What the rule will not accept is communications cable laid directly against open power wiring with nothing between them.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma practice is stricter than the code here: in a stud bay, drill separate holes and keep the 2 in, and in an attic do not lay Cat 6 across a bundle of Romex and call the joist a separator. The Code itself is satisfied where the power conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly (the NM sheath counts) — the house habit keeps the 2 in anyway. If a crossing is unavoidable, cross at right angles rather than running parallel in contact, and keep the parallel distance honest everywhere else.
sections.figure_idea: A stud-bay drawing with two bored holes 2 in apart, one holding NM cable and one holding Cat 6, plus an inset showing NM's sheath counting as the separation where the rule allows it.

sections.title: Where each cable type may be used — the application tables
sections.plain_explanation:
The tables in this section are the permission slip for cable types. One table matches listed communications cables and raceways against the places they may be installed — plenums, risers, general use, dwellings — and the coaxial cable types used under Article 820 have their own application table, Table 820.154. A higher-rated cable may substitute for a lower one down the ladder; a lower-rated cable may never substitute upward. Plenum cable sits at the top of the ladder, then riser, then general-purpose, then the limited-use dwelling type.

Where each communications type may run, in one view (the application table in plain form):
• CMP — plenum spaces, and anywhere a lower type may run
• CMR — risers and general use; not plenums
• CMG and CM — general use and dwellings; not plenums or risers
• CMX — limited use in dwellings only, within the size and length limits the table sets
sections.on_the_job: When a supplier substitutes cable, check the jacket legend against the space, not against the purchase order. CMP can go almost anywhere communications cable can go; CMX cannot leave its dwelling lane. The substitution ladder is in the figure that accompanies this section in the printed book — use it rather than memory when a job mixes types.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The ladder content is correct (CMP > CMR > CMG/CM > CMX; no upward substitution). But the 2020 edition restructured Chapter 8: Article 800 became the general article and communications circuits moved to Article 805. I could not confirm first-hand whether the 2020 Table 800.154(a) also carries the CATV (coax) types, which would make the page's statement that coax "has its own application table, Table 820.154" a 2017 holdover. Check the 2020 table titles and contents, then fix the cross-reference. Also add that CMX is limited to dwellings, raceways and short exposed runs per the table conditions.

sections.title: The cable types themselves — CMP, CMR, CMG, CM, CMX
sections.plain_explanation:
This section defines the listed communications cable types by how they behave in fire. Type CMP is the plenum type, tested for low flame spread and smoke in air-handling spaces. Type CMR is the riser type, for vertical runs between floors, and Types CMG and CM are general-purpose types for ordinary horizontal runs. Type CMX is the limited-use type, restricted in size and use, and at home mainly in one- and two-family dwellings. Conductors in these cables are copper, other than in coaxial constructions handled under Article 820. The letters say nothing about speed or category — a CMP Cat 5e and a CM Cat 6 are rated by fire behavior, not performance.

• 800.179: Moved hybrid power and communications cable general requirements to Article 800 with the other communication cable types.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the jacket before you pull: the type letters decide where the cable may go, and the category marking decides what it can carry. Do not let a cheap roll of CMX talk you into a commercial riser. Keep one shelf rule in your head: plenum space, CMP; between floors, CMR; same floor, CM or CMG; house, CM or CMX within its limits.

sections.title: Grounding hardware has to be listed
sections.plain_explanation: Where bonding or grounding is required, the devices used to connect a shield, sheath, or other non-current-carrying metallic member of a cable to a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor must be listed — or be part of listed equipment. It is a short listing rule, and it closes a gap the rest of the article leaves open: 800.100 specifies the conductor itself — its material, its size, its length, and where it may land — while this section governs the clamp or fitting that joins the cable's metal to that conductor. A primary protector or network interface device with its own grounding terminal satisfies the rule through its listing; a random piece of hardware does not.
sections.on_the_job: Use the grounding terminal built into the protector or interface device, or a listed grounding clamp made for bonding a cable shield or sheath. A hose clamp, a sheet-metal screw driven through the sheath, or an unmarked clamp off the hardware shelf is not a listed grounding device — and the fitting at the entrance is exactly where a sharp inspector looks first.

sections.title: Communications raceways and cable routing assemblies — the listing rules
sections.plain_explanation: This section is the listing home for the two support systems Article 800 builds communications installations with: communications raceways — the enclosed nonmetallic channels defined in Article 100, close cousins of ENT — and cable routing assemblies, the single or multiple channels that support high densities of cable. The raceway rules follow the same three fire levels as the cables themselves — plenum, riser, and general-purpose — and the section carries two marking tables, Table 800.182(a) for cable routing assemblies and Table 800.182(b) for communications raceways, so the level is printed on the product. One point installers miss: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it. A plenum communications raceway installed in an air-handling space under 300.22(C) still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable — the raceway and the cable are each matched to the space on their own.
sections.on_the_job: Read the print on the raceway before you hang it: plenum level for air-handling ceilings, riser level for vertical shafts, general-purpose for ordinary runs. Nonmetallic communications raceways are installed under the ENT rules this section points to — bends, supports, and joints per 362.24 through 362.56 — and cable routing assemblies support their cable at the intervals the listing allows. Where the space demands plenum, both the raceway and the cable in it must be plenum level; one out of two does not pass.

sections.title: Article 805 — Communications circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 805 is where the old pre-2020 Article 800 went to live. It covers the traditional communications circuits — the telephone-style circuits that run from the service provider's demarcation point to the customer's communications equipment — and the specific rules for those circuits that Article 800 does not already state generally. Its working topics:
• Which circuits need a primary protector, and where it goes (805.90)
• How the metallic sheath of an entering cable is grounded or interrupted at the entrance (805.93)
• The one communications outlet every new dwelling unit owes (805.156)
If Article 800 is the chapter's foundation, Article 805 is the phone-and-data entrance built on it.
sections.on_the_job: Most of Sharma's houses touch this article lightly: a demarc, a protector, a bond, and one outlet. On a new house in Sanford the whole 805 job is the demarc box on the garage wall, the provider's primary protector bonded under 800.100 with a run of about 6 ft to the intersystem bonding termination, the entering cable's sheath bonded at that same point, and one communications outlet roughed in and cabled back to the demarc. The failures are just as light — no protector where one is required, a sheath left floating, no outlet roughed in. Catch them at rough-in, when they are still cheap.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. NEC 2023 applies in Florida only to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.), so until then a 2023 study book may show different Chapter 8 numbering or wording.

sections.why_it_exists: A communications circuit is a wire that starts miles away, on poles and in plant the building owner does not control, and ends at a phone or a modem inside. Lightning and accidental contact with power conductors ride that wire indoors. Article 805 is the entrance discipline that stops the energy at the door: a protector to shunt it, a sheath grounded or interrupted so it cannot carry a surge deep into the building, and a bond that ties it all to the same earth as the power service.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is citing 800.156 for the dwelling-unit outlet. That was the pre-2020 address; the 2020 reorganization moved the rule to 805.156, and older checklists and study guides still carry the old number. Second trap: treating Article 800 as the whole story for a phone circuit. Article 800 states the general rules; the circuit-specific duties — protectors, sheath, the outlet — live in 805.

Metallic sheath of the entering cable left floating — neither grounded per 800.100 nor interrupted by an insulating joint (805.93).
New dwelling unit finished with no communications outlet cabled back to the demarcation point (805.156).

sections.title: Scope of communications circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
This short section fixes what Article 805 covers: communications circuits and the equipment on them. A communications circuit, as the chapter defines it, is the path that extends service from the communications utility or service provider up to and including the customer's own communications equipment.
• Phone and provider data circuits and their entrance equipment: Article 805, with the general rules of Article 800.
• Inside wiring that is really power-limited control or signaling work: Article 725 in Chapter 7 instead.
The same physical cable can fall under different articles depending on what system it serves, so the system, not the jacket color, decides.
sections.on_the_job: When a low-voltage scope is handed to you, ask what system each run serves before you pick an article. Phone and provider data entrance: 805 and 800. Door access, HVAC controls, and most security signaling: usually 725. On a Florida small-commercial fit-out, the same spool of Cat 6 can feed a provider phone jack in the morning (805) and a thermostat after lunch (725) — the paperwork, separation, and inspection standard change with the system, not the spool. Guessing the article is how separation and listing rules get crossed.

sections.why_it_exists: Each article carries its own separation, listing, and cable rules. Wire a control circuit under the communications rules — or a phone entrance under the control rules — and the installation can be legal-looking and still wrong: wrong cable type, wrong separation from power, wrong protection at the entrance. The scope line is what keeps the two worlds sorted.

Low-voltage scope priced and roughed in with one article assumed for every run.

sections.title: Circuits that require primary protectors — and the 4-inch rule outside
sections.plain_explanation: This section works with 805.90: it identifies the communications circuits that require primary protectors and sets conditions on the wiring that feeds them. Its part (A) covers the drop and entrance conductors used to extend circuits to a building, which must be listed for the purpose. Its part (B) carries a number crews miss: specified unshielded communications wires and cables installed on the outside of a building must be separated at least 4 in from open electric light or power wiring that is not in a raceway or a cable assembly, subject to the alternatives and exceptions the section allows. Its part (C) covers circuits entering the building ahead of the primary protector, which must be protected by a bushing or metal raceway unless an exception applies, such as entry through masonry or a listed fuseless-protector arrangement.
sections.on_the_job: The 4 in rule is about exposed wiring on the outside of the building — it is not the 2 in indoor separation of 800.133(A)(2), and the two numbers are not interchangeable. Where a drop runs down an exterior wall near open power wiring, check this section before assuming the indoor rule covers it. And do not run unprotected conductors into the building ahead of the protector through a plain hole in wood framing.

sections.title: Primary protectors — where they are required and where they go
sections.plain_explanation: A listed primary protector is required on each communications circuit that is exposed to lightning or to possible contact with power conductors operating above the threshold the section sets. The protector is an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground, mounted as the listing directs, with its terminals marked for line and ground. It must sit in, on, or immediately next to the building served, as close as practicable to where the circuit enters, and it must not be placed in a hazardous (classified) location or near easily ignitible material. The section also recognizes fused and fuseless protector designs and provides for secondary protectors inside, in series between the primary protector and the equipment.
sections.on_the_job: Short protector ground, short trouble: mount the protector at the entrance and bond it under 800.100 with the shortest honest run. If a circuit arrives with no protector and it is exposed, that is a stop-and-call item for the provider or the lead — not a detail to wave through at trim.

sections.title: Grounding or interrupting the cable sheath at the entrance
sections.plain_explanation: The non-current-carrying metallic sheath members of a communications cable entering a building must be dealt with at the entrance: either grounded following 800.100, or interrupted by an insulating joint or an equivalent device, as near as practicable to the point where the cable enters. A floating metallic sheath is a long antenna that delivers surge energy deep into the building. Grounding it at the entrance, or breaking its continuity there with an insulating joint, keeps that energy outside the living space. Section 805.93 gives exactly those two choices — there is no third option of leaving the sheath floating.
sections.on_the_job: At the demarc of an Orlando duplex rewire, the entering communications cable's shield disappears into the wall unbonded and there is no insulating joint — flag it before anything gets closed up. The fix at the entrance: bond the sheath per 800.100 with a 14 AWG minimum conductor to the intersystem bonding termination, or fit an insulating joint at the entry point. This is the communications twin of the coax rule in 820.93 — same entrance, same idea.

sections.why_it_exists: The sheath is bonded to the outside plant, so it arrives at the wall carrying whatever the outside world put on it — lightning energy, fault voltage, induced surges. If that metal runs unbroken and ungrounded into the building, the energy goes looking for a path through equipment and people indoors. Dealing with the sheath at the entrance keeps the energy at the wall, where it belongs.

sections.exam_trap: The sheath can be grounded anywhere convenient inside the building — say, at the far-end equipment rack. Wrong. 805.93 puts the treatment as near as practicable to the point of entry. Ground it deep inside and the surge energy still travels the full length of the building to get there.

sections.title: One communications outlet in every new dwelling
sections.plain_explanation: For new construction, every dwelling unit gets at least one communications outlet, installed in a readily accessible area inside the dwelling and cabled back to the service provider demarcation point. This is the rule that used to live at 800.156 before the 2020 reorganization moved it here, which is why older checklists and study guides still cite the old number. One outlet is the floor, not a design: Sharma's builders routinely want data and coax at several rooms, but the Code's own minimum is this single, cabled, accessible outlet.
sections.on_the_job: Rough it in even when the buyer has not picked a provider — a cabled outlet at the demarc is the requirement, not a live dial tone. Put it somewhere genuinely accessible, not buried behind a fixed appliance. And when an old Sharma checklist says 800.156, translate it: in the 2020 book it is 805.156.

sections.title: Article 810 — Radio and television equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Article 810 covers antenna systems: receiving antennas for radio and television, satellite dishes, their masts and lead-in conductors, and amateur and citizen-band transmitting and receiving stations. Uniquely in this chapter, Article 810 is not covered by the general rules of Article 800 — it stands alone, and its own grounding section, 810.21, is the complete recipe for bonding an antenna system. Its concerns are the ones Florida weather writes large: lightning, wind-blown lead-ins, and keeping antenna wiring clear of power conductors.
sections.on_the_job: A dish or antenna job is a grounding job with a picture at the end of it. Price and plan the mast bond, the discharge unit, and the run to a legal grounding point before anyone climbs. If a mast stands within 5 ft of a swimming pool, it also has to bond to the pool's equipotential grid — see the pool rules in Chapter 6.
sections.florida_note: Florida's lightning exposure makes 810.21 the most safety-critical page in this article here. Local amendments and insurer requirements on existing lightning protection systems vary; confirm with the AHJ on larger homes.

sections.title: Grounding the mast and its supporting structure
sections.plain_explanation:
Outdoor antenna masts, and the metal structures that support antennas, must be grounded following 810.21.
• The mast bonding or grounding conductor is sized by 810.21 — not smaller than 10 AWG copper (810.21(H)).
• There is one narrow escape: an antenna and its supporting mast or structure that sit inside a zone of protection — the area sheltered by a lightning protection system, described with a 150 ft radius rolling sphere in the lightning standard — are not required to be grounded under this section.
Outside that protected zone, which means nearly every ordinary house dish and mast Sharma will meet, the mast gets its 810.21 bond, full stop.
sections.on_the_job: Do not let “the dish is small” talk you out of the mast bond. Look for a nearby lightning protection system before claiming the zone-of-protection exception — on a normal subdivision house in Florida there is none, so ground the mast. Keep the bond run straight and protected, per 810.21, and land it on the building grounding system where 810.21 points.

Lightning does not have to hit it directly — a nearby strike can drive surge energy down the lead-in. sections.title: Clearances for antenna lead-in conductors
sections.plain_explanation: Lead-in conductors from an outdoor antenna have clearance rules in three directions. Attached to a building, they must be kept from swinging closer than 2 ft to conductors of circuits of 250 volts or less, and at least 10 ft from conductors of circuits over 250 volts. They must also keep at least 6 ft from lightning protection conductors. Underground lead-ins keep at least 12 in of separation from power conductors, and indoor antenna and lead-in conductors keep at least 2 in from light and power conductors. Separately, the conductors themselves are sized from the table in 810.16 by material and length — a lead-in under 35 ft can be as small as 19 AWG copper, while runs over 150 ft step up to 12 AWG copper, with copper-clad steel and bronze sizes listed alongside.
sections.on_the_job: Route the lead-in like it will move in wind, because in a Florida storm it will: the clearance is to the swung position, not the calm-day position. Keep the indoor tail 2 in off power wiring, the same number as 800.133(A)(2). Long spans need the bigger wire from the 810.16 table, not whatever is on the truck.

sections.title: Antenna discharge units
sections.plain_explanation:
Each lead-in conductor from an outdoor antenna gets its own listed antenna discharge unit, or an equivalent means the section allows. The unit's job is to drain static charges off the antenna system before they reach the equipment inside. Placement has three parts:
• As near as practicable to the point where the lead-in enters the building — inside or outside the wall
• Not near combustible material
• Not in a hazardous (classified) location
A discharge unit with nowhere to drain is decoration: the unit itself must be bonded or grounded following 810.21, which is what gives the drained charge somewhere to go.
sections.on_the_job: A Lake Mary house has two lead-ins: a roof antenna for local channels and the dish. That means two discharge units, mounted on the outside wall right where the lead-ins enter, each bonded with 10 AWG copper down to the intersystem bonding termination — about a 9 ft run, straight. The dish lead-in came with a factory grounding block; we checked its listing before counting it as the discharge unit instead of assuming the block was listed for that duty. One unit per lead-in, at the entrance, bonded per 810.21 — that is the whole checklist.
sections.why_it_exists: An antenna and its lead-in are a collector: wind-driven rain and dust build static charge on them, and a nearby lightning strike induces a surge on the wire. Without a discharge unit at the entrance, that energy rides the lead-in straight to the tuner, the TV, and whatever else shares the rack — and can arc inside the wall on the way. The unit bleeds the charge to ground at the door instead of letting it hunt for a path indoors.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is one discharge unit for the whole antenna system, mounted wherever the lead-ins happen to end up — a distribution block in the attic, say. Section 810.20 wants a listed unit for each lead-in conductor, placed as near as practicable to the point of entrance. Second trap: assuming the factory grounding block on a satellite lead-in automatically qualifies. It serves only if it is listed for the discharge-unit role.

sections.title: The antenna bonding and grounding recipe, (A) through (K)
sections.plain_explanation: This section is the complete set of rules for the conductors that bond an antenna mast and its discharge unit to ground. The conductor must be copper, aluminum, copper-clad steel, bronze, or a similar corrosion-resistant conductive material — copper-clad aluminum is not on the 810.21(A) list — solid or stranded, and it does not have to be insulated. It must be securely fastened, protected where it is exposed to physical damage, and run in as straight a line as practicable, inside or outside the building. It lands where the section's electrode rules point — first at the intersystem bonding termination where one exists, otherwise at the nearest accessible point on the building grounding electrode system or the other listed points, and in a building with no grounding means, at an electrode described in 250.52. Size and the bonding of separate electrodes get their own pages next, because they are the two numbers inspectors actually measure. Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum conductors must not be placed in direct contact with masonry or the earth, and where installed outdoors must not come within 18 inches of the earth.
sections.on_the_job: Straight, short, protected, and landed at a listed point — run this bond the way you would a grounding electrode conductor, because that is what it is. Take the intersystem bonding termination when the house has one (L-060); it was installed for exactly this conductor. Sharp bends and a tour of the attic are the classic fails.

sections.title: Antenna bonding conductor size — 10 AWG copper
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 810.21(H) sets the floor for the conductor that bonds an antenna mast or an antenna discharge unit to ground. It cannot be smaller than:
• 10 AWG copper
• 17 AWG copper-clad steel or bronze
• 8 AWG aluminum
The 17 AWG size looks impossibly thin until you know what it is: the messenger-style wire molded into the jacket of much satellite coax, copper-clad steel or bronze, which is why a factory dish lead-in can carry its own bond. Ten AWG copper is noticeably heavier than the 14 AWG floor for a communications protector bond in 800.100(A). That is deliberate — antennas sit up in the lightning, and the Code sizes their bond accordingly. The conductor itself follows the rest of 810.21: approved materials, securely fastened, protected from damage, and run as straight as practicable.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma house in Ocala, the dish and an over-the-air antenna share one mast. The bond is 10 AWG bare copper, run straight down the wall about 22 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main. The dish lead-in arrived with the molded 17 AWG messenger, and it checked out as copper-clad steel, continuous to the grounding block — legal, but the 10 AWG run is still the one we pulled for the mast itself. If a helper reaches for the 14 AWG spool from the phone-protector work, stop him: that spool is for 800.100(A) bonds, not antennas.
sections.why_it_exists: A mast and a dish collect static charge and sit where lightning energy arrives first. The bond is the path that carries that energy to earth. A conductor that is too small can be damaged by the very surge it is supposed to drain, and a thin corroded wire can part without anyone noticing — leaving the discharge unit draining into air while the next surge looks for a path through the receiver and the house wiring instead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 14 AWG, because 14 AWG is the Chapter 8 bonding floor everyone remembers. That floor belongs to 800.100(A), for protector and sheath bonds. Section 810.21(H) sets its own, heavier floor for antennas: 10 AWG copper. The second trap runs the other way — rejecting a 17 AWG messenger as too small to be legal. It is legal, but only as copper-clad steel or bronze, never as plain copper or copper-clad aluminum.

Aluminum bonding conductor run in contact with the earth — 810.21 bars aluminum from earth and masonry contact and keeps it 18 in above the earth outdoors.

sections.title: Bonding a separate antenna electrode — 6 AWG again
sections.plain_explanation: If a separate ground rod or other electrode is installed to serve the radio and television equipment, it cannot stand alone. It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system with a conductor no smaller than 6 AWG copper or the equivalent. This is the same anti-islanding rule as 800.100(D): one building, one earth reference, no matter how many systems drive their own rods. A separate electrode is permitted; a separate, unbonded electrode is a hazard wearing a ground rod's clothes.
sections.on_the_job: Driven a dish rod because the service was far away? The job ends when the 6 AWG bond ties it back to the power grounding system, not when the rod disappears below grade. Budget that conductor run when the dish location is chosen — on a wide Florida lot it is often the longest wire in the whole antenna job, and finding an unbonded rod on a service call means the original job was never finished.

sections.why_it_exists: Two electrodes that are not tied together do not sit at the same voltage. In a surge or a nearby lightning strike, thousands of volts can appear between them (800.100(D)) — and the equipment connected to both systems, or a person touching it, becomes the path that equalizes them. The 6 AWG bond keeps every rod at one reference so the difference never builds.
inspection_fails: Separate dish rod driven and left unbonded to the power grounding system.
Bond run made with a conductor smaller than 6 AWG copper.
Rod “grounded” to a hose bibb or an isolated pipe instead of the grounding electrode system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: “A second rod makes the ground better, so bonding it back is optional — two grounds are better than one.” Wrong. An unbonded second rod is worse than none: it creates a second earth reference that can sit thousands of volts away from the first in a surge. 810.21(J) allows the rod only with the 6 AWG bond.

sections.title: Amateur and citizen-band transmitting stations
sections.plain_explanation: Transmitting antennas for amateur (ham) and citizen-band stations get the receiving-station rules plus their own. Each outdoor antenna lead-in conductor needs an antenna discharge unit or another suitable means of draining static, under 810.57. The bonding and grounding conductors then follow 810.58: the protective bonding or grounding conductor must be at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG copper, bronze, or copper-clad steel, while the operating bonding or grounding conductor cannot be smaller than 14 AWG copper or its equivalent. These stations also still owe the mast grounding of 810.15 and the installation rules of Part III of this article.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets this mostly in custom homes with a ham shack roughed into a study or garage. Treat the radio room's ground as a system: discharge unit at the entrance, protective bond at 10 AWG minimum, operating bond at 14 AWG minimum, all tied to the one building grounding reference.

sections.title: Article 820 — Community antenna television and radio distribution (coax)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 820 covers coaxial cable systems that distribute television and radio signals — cable TV, and closed-circuit television of the same construction. The system's defining part is the coax itself: a center conductor inside a metallic outer shield, and that shield is where this article's safety rules concentrate. The shield of a coax arriving from outside must be grounded at the entrance, the cable types are listed in this article, and the general rules of Article 800 — separation, installation, fire — layer on top unless 820 changes them. Note what 820 does not require: unlike a telephone circuit, a coax entrance is not required to have a primary protector, though if one is installed it must be listed and applied at the entrance.
sections.on_the_job: For Sharma this is the cable company's drop, the grounding block on the side of the house, and the coax distribution inside. Our scope is usually the bond at the block and clean, separated inside runs — the provider owns their drop up to the demarc, but the bond at our service is everybody's inspection item.

sections.title: Grounding the coax shield at the point of entrance
sections.plain_explanation:
The outer conductive shield of a coaxial cable supplied to a building must be grounded as close as practicable to the point where the cable enters, following the conductor rules of 820.100. The grounding connection can be made where the cable terminates outside the building or just inside it — the point of entrance can effectively be extended by a grounded metal raceway — but 'as close as practicable' is the standard either way. A coax shield left floating at a house is the single most common Chapter 8 defect in residential work.

The conductor rules it points to are spelled out on the next page (820.100): not smaller than 14 AWG, never required to be larger than 6 AWG, and at a one- or two-family dwelling not longer than 20 ft — the chapter's standard entrance numbers, so a coax bond is checked with the same tape measure as a telephone bond.
sections.on_the_job: Find the grounding block before trim-out and verify the bond is actually landed, at the service or another 820.100 point — a block screwed to the wall with an empty ground lug is a fail waiting for a surge. Keep the bond conductor short; the entrance is not the place for a scenic route.
sections.figure_idea: An exterior wall detail: coax drop, grounding block at the entrance, and a short bonding conductor to the intersystem bonding termination.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The substance (ground the coax shield as close as practicable to entrance; 14 AWG min, 6 AWG max required, 20 ft max at one-/two-family dwellings) matches the Chapter 8 pattern. But the page sends the conductor rules to "820.100", while C8-840.93 sends the same rules to "800.100". After the 2020 Chapter 8 reorganization, the general bonding/grounding recipe lives in 800.100. sections.title: Coax bonding and grounding conductors
sections.plain_explanation: This section sends the coax shield's bonding and grounding conductor back to the same recipe as 800.100: copper or another corrosion-resistant material, no smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the coax's outer shield but never required to exceed 6 AWG. In a one- or two-family dwelling the conductor must be as short as practicable and no more than 20 ft; if that length cannot be met, a separate electrode may be installed and then bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with at least 6 AWG, under part (D). For coax systems that never leave the building and are isolated from outside plant, an exception allows the shield to be bonded through an equipment grounding conductor of a listed type instead.
sections.on_the_job: Same numbers as the phone protector, because the Code means them to rhyme: 14 AWG floor, 6 AWG ceiling, 20 ft at a house, 6 AWG bond for a separate rod. If the cable system is purely internal — a camera system that never exits — read the exception before driving anything. Otherwise, bond at the entrance like every other system in this chapter.

sections.title: Installing coaxial cable inside the building
sections.plain_explanation: Listed coaxial cable inside a building follows the installation framework of Article 800 as this section applies it: the right cable type for the space — plenum, riser, or general use — chosen from this article's cable list and the application tables. There is a distance rule that drives most house work: unlisted outside-plant coax may come into a building only a limited distance — 50 ft from the point of entrance — before listed cable is required, under 820.48. Past that point, the run must be listed coax of a type permitted for the space it passes through.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the entrance path on long custom homes: if the distribution panel sits more than 50 ft of cable run from where the drop enters, the whole run needs listed cable, not the provider's outdoor spool. In commercial ceilings and shafts, treat coax exactly like communications cable for fire rating — CMP in plenums, CATVR-type riser cable between floors.

sections.title: Separation for coaxial cable
sections.plain_explanation: Coaxial cable obeys the same separation discipline as the rest of the chapter. It may not share a raceway or box with electric light and power conductors, it may not be supported from a raceway that contains power conductors, and it keeps at least 2 in from light and power conductors unless those conductors are in a raceway or in a sheathed cable assembly such as nonmetallic-sheathed, armored, or UF cable. Article 800's 800.133 states the general rule; this section carries it into the coax world, so a helper who learns one has learned both.
sections.on_the_job: Run coax in its own holes, on its own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as Cat 6. The classic fail is a coax home-run bundle zip-tied along an EMT or draped over a Romex bundle in the attic. Separate supports cost minutes; a failed inspection costs a return trip.

sections.title: Where each coaxial cable type may be used — Table 820.154
sections.plain_explanation: Article 820 sorts coaxial cable into four listed types, and the ladder runs in one direction. CATVP, the plenum type, sits at the top; CATVR, the riser type, below it; then CATV, the general-purpose type; and CATVX, the limited-use type, at the bottom. Table 820.154 carries the substitution hierarchy: a higher type may be used in place of a lower one — plenum for riser, riser for general — and a lower type may never be substituted upward. Which type a given space demands is set by the article's installation and listing rules — not by the jacket color, and not by what the supplier shipped.
sections.on_the_job: Coax home runs through a return-air plenum in a light-commercial ceiling in Winter Park: CATVP, or a listed raceway — the CATV reel from the truck does not become legal because the ceiling is almost never opened. Before the pull, read the jacket legend on every reel and stage the plenum reels separately from the general-purpose stock.

sections.plain_explanation: 820.179 lists the coaxial cable types and their markings. CATVP is the plenum type, CATVR the riser type, CATV the general-purpose type, and CATVX the limited-use type, restricted to dwellings and raceway. sections.on_the_job: CATVX is the trap type: fine in the dwelling work it is listed for, a violation pulled into a commercial riser. On a Winter Park strip-center rewire, the reel marked CATVX stays on the truck — the riser pulls get CATVR. Check the legend before the pull, not at the inspection.

sections.title: Article 830 — Network-powered broadband systems
sections.plain_explanation: Article 830 covers broadband systems where the network itself sends the power: the provider's network powers the network interface unit at the customer's building, over the same plant that carries the signal. Because power arrives from off the premises on a communications cable, this article is stricter at the entrance than plain CATV — its circuits get primary protection, and its shields, protectors, and interface-unit enclosures all get grounded. The general rules of Article 800 still layer underneath, and 830 borrows the 800.100 grounding recipe for its conductors. Sharma meets 830 as the powered cable-broadband entrance on commercial and multi-dwelling work more than on single houses.
sections.on_the_job: Recognize the powered entrance by the network interface unit and the provider's powering arrangement, not by the shape of the cable. Once you know power is coming in on it, the protector and grounding pages that follow are not optional reading. Keep hands off the provider's powered plant beyond the demarc — that side is theirs.

sections.title: Primary protectors on network-powered broadband circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Because a network-powered broadband circuit brings both signal and network power in from outside plant, each of its conductors gets primary protection at the entrance, in the pattern of the protector rules used across this chapter (805.90):
• A listed primary protector — an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground.
• Mounted in, on, or immediately next to the building, as close as practicable to the point of entrance.
• Ahead of the network interface unit and the inside distribution.
The protector deals with the same two threats as at a telephone entrance: lightning energy riding in on the outside plant, and accidental contact between that plant and power conductors out on the poles.
sections.on_the_job: If a powered broadband entrance has no protector, treat it like a phone entrance with no protector: a provider-side correction to raise before the installation is signed off. On a Florida home or small office where the cable provider lands a network-powered drop, check the entrance before trim-out: protector present, ahead of the interface unit, and grounded — the shield, the protector, and the interface enclosure all land on the one building grounding reference (830.93). Sharma's part is usually the bond and the space: leave the protector accessible and its grounding path short and straight.

sections.why_it_exists: Outside plant is exposed plant. A lightning strike blocks away, or a fallen power conductor touching the drop, can put surge energy on a circuit that runs straight to equipment inside — and broadband circuits carry network power as well as signal. The protector gives that energy a path to ground at the door instead of through the building.

sections.title: Grounding shields, protectors, and the interface unit
sections.plain_explanation: Three things at a network-powered broadband entrance must be grounded: the metallic shield of the broadband cable, the primary protector, and the metallic enclosure of the network interface unit. Section 830.93 sends all three to the grounding conductor rules of 800.100 — the same rules that ground the other Chapter 8 systems. Everything metallic that the outside plant touches at the entrance ends up on the one building grounding reference: shield, protector ground, and enclosure alike. Bond only the shield and the job is two-thirds done; the enclosure is not optional. The grounding conductor itself follows 800.100 for size, routing and where it may land.
sections.on_the_job: New townhome rough-in, Kissimmee: the provider's coax lands on the primary protector at the garage demarc and the interface unit mounts beside it. Bond all three — shield, protector, enclosure — with 14 AWG minimum copper, run short and straight to the intersystem bonding termination, per 800.100. Photograph the entrance assembly at rough-in; broadband entrances get buried behind provider equipment fast, and the photo is your proof at final.

Lightning and utility surges ride that path, and the protector can only dump energy it can reach ground with. Any metallic part left floating at the entrance — the enclosure is the one most often skipped — can sit at a dangerous voltage next to grounded equipment, waiting for a hand to bridge the gap.
