sections.title: Broadband bonding and grounding conductors
sections.plain_explanation: The bonding and grounding conductors for a network-powered broadband entrance follow the same dimensional rules as the rest of the chapter: not smaller than 14 AWG, not required to exceed 6 AWG, as short as practicable, and no more than 20 ft in a one- or two-family dwelling. The section carries the same escape hatch as 800.100 and 820.100 — where the length cannot be met, a separate electrode is permitted, and its exception structure requires that electrode to be bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with a conductor of at least 6 AWG. By this point in the chapter the pattern should be familiar, because the Code intends it to be one pattern repeated.
sections.on_the_job: Do not re-derive the numbers at a broadband entrance; they are the chapter's numbers. Fourteen to six AWG, twenty feet at a house, six AWG to bond a separate rod. If you know 800.100 cold, you already know this page.

sections.title: Separation for network-powered broadband cable
sections.figure_idea: Open-run cross-section: broadband cable held 2 in from a power run; raceway exception beside it.
sections.plain_explanation:
Broadband cable under Article 830 keeps the same separation discipline as the rest of Chapter 8.
• In a raceway, box, or enclosure, it does not run with electric light and power conductors except where 830.133's own conditions are met — a permanent barrier or listed divider between the two systems is the classic way those conditions are satisfied.
• In open runs, it keeps the chapter's familiar 2 in separation from power conductors.
• The 2 in is not required where one side or the other is in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly, or where a continuous, firmly fixed nonconductor separates the two.
The network power on a broadband circuit makes the separation worth more, not less: this is the one communications-style cable whose network side arrives carrying power from outside the building.
sections.why_it_exists: Every other communications cable in the chapter is a guest in the building; a network-powered broadband cable arrives already energized from the network side. A cross-contact, a crushed jacket or a fault in a shared box can put that outside power — or building power — onto inside wiring and equipment that nobody expects to be live. Separation is the cheap, permanent insurance that the two systems never meet.
sections.on_the_job: Broadband entrance and inside runs: own holes, own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as 800.133 and 820.133, because the Code intends one pattern for the whole chapter. On a Kissimmee rental rehab, the broadband drop crossed the garage ceiling 2 in clear of the open power runs; at the one place it had to cross the EMT feeder, the raceway itself satisfied the rule, so the crossing needed no extra spacing.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that broadband is 'just cable TV,' so it can share a box or raceway with power like any low-voltage cable. Wrong. It does not share a raceway, box or enclosure with power conductors except under 830.133's own conditions — and because the network side arrives carrying power, the separation matters more here, not less.

sections.title: Article 840 — Premises-powered broadband systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 840 covers broadband systems where the power is supplied at the premises instead of by the network — the classic case is fiber arriving at an optical network terminal that plugs into a local receptacle. The fiber itself carries no metallic path and no power, which changes the entrance picture: there is no outside metallic shield arriving on glass, and the protection focus shifts to any metallic members that do enter and to the terminal equipment at the premises. Article 840 works with the optical fiber rules of Article 770 in Chapter 7 for the fiber cable itself, and sends its grounding questions to the Chapter 8 pattern in the protector rules at 805.90 and the entrance bonding and grounding rules at 800.100 as the specific sections direct. It is the shortest article in the chapter and, for Sharma, mostly a fiber-to-the-home entrance on new custom work.

One census note, so nobody hunts for pages that do not exist: in NEC 2020 this chapter ends here. Chapter 8 has exactly six articles — 800, 805, 810, 820, 830 and 840 — and the article numbers 850 through 890 are not assigned in the 2020 edition. Optical fiber cable rules are not in this chapter at all in 2020; they live in Article 770 in Chapter 7. If a study aid or a newer book lists communications articles above 840, it is describing a different edition, and its section numbers will not match this one.
sections.on_the_job: On a fiber entrance, find what is actually metallic: a metallic strength member, a locate wire, or a hybrid cable changes the grounding answer, while pure dielectric fiber does not get a bond it does not need. The ONT still needs its premises power planned — a receptacle at the right place is Sharma's scope even when the fiber is not.

sections.title: Grounding at a premises-powered broadband entrance
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a premises-powered broadband cable arriving at a building has metallic members that require grounding — a metallic shield, strength member, or similar conductive part — those members are grounded following the chapter's entrance-grounding pattern, as close as practicable to the point of entrance. The rule exists for the hybrid and metallic-bearing entrance cables, not for dielectric fiber, which has nothing conductive to ground. Grounding follows the conductor and landing-point rules the article references back into the general Chapter 8 framework.

The conductor behind that bond is the chapter's standard one, from the 800.100 recipe this article works through: copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, not smaller than 14 AWG and never required to be larger than 6 AWG, run as short as practicable — and at a one- or two-family dwelling not over 20 ft, with the separate-electrode route and its 6 AWG bond back to the power grounding electrode system (800.100(D)) when that length cannot be met. Same numbers as the telephone and coax entrances, applied here to the metallic members that actually exist.
sections.on_the_job: Inspect the actual cable construction before deciding there is nothing to bond. If the entrance cable carries a metallic member, bond it at the entrance like every other system in this chapter. If it is all-dielectric, say so on the job record instead of leaving the next crew to guess why there is no bond.

sections.title: Premises-powered broadband circuits and power circuits — 840.160
sections.plain_explanation:
840.160 is the section that faces the question the rest of Chapter 8 answers with separation: what happens when premises-powered broadband communications circuits meet electric light and power circuits. The chapter's default does not change — communications and power are kept apart under the installation rules that apply to the broadband system — and 840.160 works as the narrow, conditioned door, addressing the combinations the article itself describes, such as circuits associated with the same equipment. It is an exception path with conditions, not a general permission to land broadband and power in the same box because both serve the same terminal.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 840.160: Changed the reference from Section 725.154(A) to Section 722.135 as cable substitution, and installation requirements are now in Article 722.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: At an optical network terminal: the power supply and the broadband drops each follow their own rules, and any combined enclosure or shared path has to be one the equipment listing and 840.160 actually describe. When in doubt, separate — separation is never the violation.
